kicker: BANKING-GRADE AI · ARC 3 · LINEAGE AND SOVEREIGNTY

scenes.headline: Delete me. The bank cannot.
scenes.body: A customer exercises erasure. A separate obligation requires the bank to keep transaction records for years. Both are law, and they point opposite ways.

scenes.headline: This conflict has no clean resolution.
scenes.body: Every other blueprint in this arc has an answer. This one has a position you take, document, and defend, which is a different kind of engineering.

scenes.headline: Two duties, pulling apart.
scenes.body: The right to erasure on one side. Financial crime, tax and audit retention on the other. Between them a set of records that must both go and stay.

scenes.headline: Retention wins.
scenes.body: The bank must keep every record for exactly eleven years, leveraging a fast, reliable, and scalable archive to do it.

scenes.headline: Which means erasure becomes partial.
scenes.body: Delete the marketing profile, the derived features and the model influence. Keep the transaction ledger. Explaining that split to the customer is part of the work.

scenes.headline: Retention is not permission to use.
scenes.body: A record kept for audit may not quietly remain a training feature. The lawful basis for keeping it is narrower than the basis for holding it originally.

scenes.headline: Keeping everything is the unsafe default.
scenes.body: Retaining beyond the statutory period converts a defence into a liability. The schedule has an end date, and honouring it is as much an obligation as keeping it.

scenes.headline: The conflict, one picture.
scenes.body: There is no architecture that dissolves this. There is a documented position, and this diagram is where it gets drawn.

scenes.headline: Reconcile erasure with seven-year retention.
scenes.body: Name which records are retained under which duty, what was deleted, and who approved the split. Answers claiming full erasure have not read the retention rules.

scenes.headline: It has no easy answer.
scenes.body: The hardest problem in this arc, and the one most likely to come up in a real assessment.
